blocks.text: Why changing a branch can break a value

We work with LLVM intermediate representation (IR), the instructions between source code and machine code. A function body is divided into basic blocks: straight-line instruction sequences ending in a terminator such as a branch or return. Branches connect blocks into a control-flow graph (CFG). A predecessor is a block with an incoming edge to the block we are discussing; a successor is a destination of an outgoing edge. An instruction defines a result when it produces a value, and another instruction uses that result when it consumes it.

Day 1 described programs. Day 2 changes how they execute. Our goal is to route decisions through one dispatcher while preserving the answers, effects, and termination of every execution covered by our support contract. This is why we cannot start by replacing all the branches: a program carries both control flow (which block runs next) and data flow (which computed values later instructions use).

Why route decisions through a dispatcher at all? Ordinary branches expose familiar shapes such as a diamond for an if/else and a back edge for a loop. Control-flow flattening aims to obscure that direct structure by making many transitions use one shared routing mechanism. We still owe the caller the same computation. This project lets us study that representation change and its costs; whether it remains difficult to analyze after optimization is a separate question.

Imagine one block computes a subtotal and another returns it. The old route guarantees that calculation happens before the return. New dispatcher edges change the routes LLVM sees. Even if our state numbers are intended to choose the right order at runtime, the rewritten IR must still obey LLVM’s rules for where each value can be used.

rows: What you should understand before coding
Existing value dependencies were designed for the old graph.
Where each value comes from and how a later use receives it.
The next block must be selected through the dispatcher.
How each old decision becomes a next-state choice.
A valid-looking graph may still compute the wrong answer.
Which structural rules and observable results must remain true.

blocks.text: The first lessons therefore concentrate on values, especially PHIs. These are preparation steps for flattening, not unrelated instruction-counting exercises. Each later lesson explains which part of the same control-and-data problem it addresses.
Task: Read this context before editing FlatteningPass. Day 1 built the plugin, statistics, CFG analysis, and eligibility checker. Day 2 starts changing eligible functions.
What are we trying to build?

A dispatcher is a block that reads a state number and uses a switch to choose the next program block. Eventually, an original branch will become “store the destination state, then branch to the dispatcher.” We have not implemented that complete transformation yet.

original entry/setup → dispatcher → selected original block
                           ↑                  |
                           └──────────────────┘
The original entry stays a one-time setup block. Its stack slots must not be allocated repeatedly in the dispatcher. Return and unreachable blocks finish their path instead of looping back.
Recall SSA and dominance

An SSA value has one definition. That definition must dominate its uses: every reachable path from entry to a use passes through the definition. Adding dispatcher edges can create new paths that violate that relationship, even if the original program never had a problem.
The memory operations you will see

rows: Allocate space for one i32 in the current function’s stack frame; the result is a pointer.
Write %x into the storage addressed by %slot; the instruction produces no result.
Read an i32 from that address; the result is a new SSA value.
Select an incoming value according to the predecessor edge used to enter the block.

i1 means one bit: 0 is false and 1 is true for a condition; i32 means a 32-bit integer bit pattern; signed interpretation comes from operations such as slt or sdiv, not from a separate signed i32 type.

An opaque pointer value: it can represent an address or the special handle returned in the coroutine example. It does not contain an i32 integer or encode a pointee type. A load/store spells out the type of value accessed separately from the pointer.

The left side names the result of this instruction. Each SSA result has one static defining instruction; input arguments are values supplied at function entry. A name is a handle for a value, not a mutable source variable or a guaranteed CPU register.

This is a typed literal: the i-prefixed part specifies the bit width, and the decimal part is the constant value. For example, a case number or stored state ID is an integer value, unlike a `%name` or `name:` label.

Everything after a semicolon on that line is a comment for the reader. The printer lists incoming blocks after preds; it is not an instruction, an execution order, or a separate edge definition. Branch/switch operands actually define the edges.

Alignment is in bytes, not elements, bits, or a value to store. An aligned alloca provides suitably aligned storage; an aligned load/store promises that its pointer meets that alignment. It does not initialize memory or change the integer read/written.

rows: Meaning and operand order in these listings

Reserve storage for the shown element type in this function invocation and produce its address, not the stored integer. `alloca i32` reserves one i32 slot. The allocation does not initialize its contents; a store must supply a value before an intended read.

`br label %B` always transfers control to block B. `br i1 %C, label %A, label %B` goes to A for true and B for false; their order matters. A branch is the block’s final instruction and produces no result. It does not execute both destinations.

Read a value from memory: in `load i32, ptr %slot`, i32 is the loaded value’s type and %slot is its address. The left-hand result gets the current contents, not another copy of the address. Each load defines a new SSA value; it does not compute the value that a missing earlier store should have supplied.

Define one value by the edge just used to enter this block. Each `[ VALUE, %PREDECESSOR ]` pairs an incoming value with its source block; it is not an array access. The PHI’s i32 type applies to every incoming value, so a literal inside a bracket does not repeat the type. PHIs go at the start of a block. On a loop’s first entry choose its entry value, and on a back edge choose its carried value. Multiple PHIs select incoming values together, rather than sequentially overwriting each other.

End this function invocation and return the typed operand to its caller. `ret i32 %v` returns the integer value, while `ret ptr ...` returns a pointer. A return does not proceed to the next printed block or automatically go back to dispatch.

Produce a value from `select i1 CONDITION, TYPE TRUE_VALUE, TYPE FALSE_VALUE`. A true condition chooses the first alternative, false the second; alternatives have the same type. This does not branch or conditionally execute the instructions that computed the operands. Here the chosen result is either a destination’s state number or the final return value.

Write memory: in `store i32 VALUE, ptr ADDRESS`, the first operand is the value and the second is the destination address. A store has an effect but no result name. Writing a state slot changes the next routing choice; writing a demotion slot transports an original program value.

Transfer control according to one integer value. The destination immediately after the condition is the default for no matching case. Each line inside `[...]` pairs a typed case constant with `label %DESTINATION`; only one destination is taken. An original switch chooses a program outcome; a dispatcher switch decodes the stored state ID. The brackets are a case list, not a runtime array.

End the block by asserting that execution never reaches this point on a defined run. Actually executing it is undefined behavior; it is not error recovery, a return, or a C++ exception. The state-machine invariant must prevent a bad stored ID from taking this default path.

blocks.text: Keep address, contents, and loaded value separate. For example, an alloca result is the address of a slot; a store writes an integer into that slot; a later load defines a new SSA name for the integer read back. The pointer name does not become the stored number. A value slot preserves program data, whereas ms.state (when present) stores a control-flow destination encoding.
Walk one concrete execution

Call merge with condition = true: take left and obtain 10; with false, take right and obtain 20. In a PHI listing join chooses the incoming constant using the predecessor edge. In a demoted listing only the executed path stores its constant, and join reads that value. In the complete machine entry selects state 0 or 1, the chosen path writes its data value then state 2, and dispatch enters join. The stored state number 2 means “run join”; it is not the result 10 or 20.

blocks.text: Before — phi original

entry:
  br i1 %condition, label %left, label %right

left:                                             ; preds = %entry
  br label %join

right:                                            ; preds = %entry
  br label %join

  %value = phi i32 [ 10, %left ], [ 20, %right ]

define i32 @merge(i1 %condition) {
entry:
  %ms.state = alloca i32, align 4
  %value.reg2mem = alloca i32, align 4
  %ms.next = select i1 %condition, i32 0, i32 1
  store i32 %ms.next, ptr %ms.state, align 4
  br label %ms.dispatch

left:                                             ; preds = %ms.dispatch
  store i32 10, ptr %value.reg2mem, align 4
  store i32 2, ptr %ms.state, align 4
  br label %ms.dispatch

right:                                            ; preds = %ms.dispatch
  store i32 20, ptr %value.reg2mem, align 4
  store i32 2, ptr %ms.state, align 4
  br label %ms.dispatch

join:                                             ; preds = %ms.dispatch
  %value.reload = load i32, ptr %value.reg2mem, align 4
  ret i32 %value.reload

ms.dispatch:                                      ; preds = %right, %left, %entry
  %ms.current = load i32, ptr %ms.state, align 4
  switch i32 %ms.current, label %ms.invalid [
    i32 0, label %left
    i32 1, label %right
    i32 2, label %join
  ]

ms.invalid:                                       ; preds = %ms.dispatch
  unreachable
}

lessons.title: Collect PHIs without changing them
lessons.summary: Understand why SSA needs a path-dependent value at a join, why changing predecessors threatens that choice, and why we collect PHIs before rewriting them.
lessons.takeaway: Preserve the incoming path’s value choice before replacing its edges.

blocks.text: Why a compiler needs a PHI at a join
Start with a familiar source-language variable. A conditional can assign that variable on either path, and code after the conditional must use whichever assignment actually happened:

LLVM commonly represents computed values in static single assignment form, or SSA: each named instruction result has one defining instruction; a function argument is a value supplied at function entry. This makes dependencies explicit. An optimizer can follow a name back to one definition instead of searching through every possible reassignment of a mutable variable. One static definition can execute many times in a loop; “single assignment” describes the IR definition, not a promise to execute it only once.

At a join, however, the available value depends on the path taken. We cannot give one SSA name two separate defining assignments. A PHI expresses that choice in one definition. In tests/ir/phi.ll, the relevant instruction is:

join:
  %value = phi i32 [ 10, %left ], [ 20, %right ]
  ret i32 %value

Read each bracket as “value, incoming predecessor.” If execution enters join from left, value is 10; if it enters from right, value is 20. The predecessor is the block whose edge was just taken. The PHI does not rerun the condition, execute both paths, or take whichever value appears first in the text. This example uses constants; real incoming values can be results computed on the different paths.
Why PHIs matter to our flattening pass

Before: left  ───────→ join     PHI can distinguish left from right.
        right ───────→ join

Later:  left/right → dispatcher → join
                               The last predecessor is now dispatcher.

If we change the edges but keep the old PHI unchanged, its incoming labels no longer describe the predecessors of join. The PHI is both a useful account of the original value choice and a dependency on the original graph. We need to preserve that choice in another form before replacing those edges.

This lesson only finds those instructions and records their addresses. The next lessons use that worklist to replace predecessor-based choices with explicit memory transfers. A count of zero means this preparation step has nothing to do; it does not mean the function has no other data-flow constraints.
Checkpoint: If join is entered from right, why must the PHI select 20? What information would disappear if the immediate predecessor became dispatcher?
Task: Collect PHI nodes in the existing FlatteningPass::run(), after the eligibility guard. This lesson does not modify IR.
The template to start with
Step 1 — Include the types and container
Instructions.h defines PHINode and other instruction subclasses. Casting.h supplies LLVM’s type checks. std::vector is a growable collection; this vector’s element type is PHINode*, not Instruction*.
Step 2 — Traverse existing instructions by reference

F is a mutable Function&. Therefore auto &BB and auto &I refer to mutable existing blocks and instructions. Plain auto would try to copy objects; const auto & would prevent collecting the mutable PHI pointers needed by the later utility.
Step 3 — Keep the result of dyn_cast

dyn_cast returns a PHINode* when the instruction is a PHI, or nullptr otherwise. The if tests that pointer. push_back copies the pointer into the vector; it does not copy or take ownership of the instruction.

lessons.title: Keep the typed pointer from dyn_cast
lessons.originalTitle: Keep the typed pointer from dyn_cast
lessons.summary: Understand the actual push_back error: a successful type test does not change the declared type of the original instruction.
lessons.takeaway: A type check is useful only if you keep the typed result you need.

blocks.text: Why the worklist needs a more specific kind of instruction

The previous lesson identified PHIs as the operations whose incoming choices must be preserved. But the loop visits every instruction: arithmetic, loads, branches, returns, and PHIs. The later PHI-demotion helper accepts a PHINode*, so the worklist must contain instructions proven to be PHIs.

A typed pointer records that knowledge in C++. Testing whether an instruction is a PHI does not change the declared type of the original loop variable. Keeping the pointer returned by dyn_cast carries the successful check into the vector and then into the transformation call. This is how the conceptual selection becomes a type-safe worklist; it creates no new IR object.
Task: Fix the pointer-type mismatch encountered while collecting PHIs. Work in the inner instruction loop from the previous lesson.
The failing template
Step 1 — Read the declared types

A PHINode derives from Instruction. Converting PHINode* to Instruction* is an upcast. The reverse needs a check: an arbitrary Instruction* might identify an add, branch, load, or return. A condition does not automatically narrow the C++ type of I.
Step 2 — Name the cast result
auto *phi = llvm::dyn_cast<llvm::PHINode>(&I);
This does not allocate a PHI. It gives a more specific pointer to the same instruction if the type matches. The draft discarded this pointer and then pushed the original, less-specific &I.
Step 3 — Append only a successful cast
Use an if-initializer-style declaration in the condition so the typed pointer is available inside the body. A null pointer skips the body.
The full corrected fragment
Observed error: phis.push_back(&I) fails because the vector needs PHINode* but &I remains Instruction*. Saving the result as phi makes the argument type match.
Verify

cmake --build build
opt -load-pass-plugin="$PWD/build/libMiniShield.so" \
  -passes='function(minishield-flatten),verify' \
  -disable-output tests/ir/phi.ll
Compilation should succeed and the phi.ll count should still be 1. We have changed C++ bookkeeping, not LLVM IR.

blocks.title: LLVM casts refine a borrowed pointer’s static type

blocks.text: A PHINode inherits from Instruction, but a vector<PHINode*> cannot accept an arbitrary Instruction*. dyn_cast<PHINode>(&I) asks LLVM’s class hierarchy whether the existing instruction is a PHI. Success returns a PHINode* to that same object; failure returns nullptr. No PHI is allocated or copied.

This is LLVM’s classof-based casting machinery, not C++ dynamic_cast and not a request to enable compiler RTTI. cast<T> asserts that the type is appropriate; dyn_cast<T> handles a possible mismatch. Use isa<T> when you only need a yes/no answer. See [LLVM casting](https://llvm.org/docs/ProgrammersManual.html#the-isa-cast-and-dyn-cast-templates).
Checkpoint: After a successful cast, do base and phi refer to two instructions or one? Who owns that instruction?
Checkpoint: Why is &I later valid for a vector<Instruction*> but invalid here? Explain the difference between a runtime type test and the static type of an expression.

blocks.text: What demotion changes, and why we want it

We have located the places where the old graph chooses a value by predecessor. Before routing those paths through a shared dispatcher, we need another way to communicate that choice. PHI demotion replaces the implicit “which incoming edge?” selection with explicit writes and reads of a shared storage slot.

Path from left:  write 10 into slot ─┐
                                    ├→ join: read slot → return result
Path from right: write 20 into slot ─┘

Only the executed path writes its incoming value for this diamond. join reads the stored value. Thus the path still determines the result, but join no longer needs a PHI mentioning left and right as its direct predecessors. This prepares the value transport for later edge changes; demotion itself does not create or connect the dispatcher.

“Demote” means lowering a selected SSA value into memory-based storage. The slot can be written on different paths; each load from it still defines its own SSA result. We are not switching LLVM out of SSA, deleting the selected computation, or merely renaming a variable.

Incoming paths arrange the writes; users read the slot.

blocks.text: Why removing PHIs is only half of preparation

A PHI is one way blocks exchange values, but ordinary instructions can also define a value in one block that another block uses. For example, entry can calculate sum, branch to exit, and have exit return sum. That function has no PHI at all.

LLVM requires an ordinary definition to dominate its uses: every entry-to-use path must pass through the definition. Think of a receipt that must be written before any reader can refer to it. Adding a dispatcher edge to the reader can create a graph route that bypasses the writer. The verifier checks the graph relationship; it does not accept “our state IDs will never choose that order” as a replacement for SSA dominance.

PHI demotion can itself produce a load whose result is used in another block. We therefore inspect ordinary cross-block dependencies after the PHI stage. This worklist finds remaining value transport to prepare, rather than assuming “no PHIs” means “safe to rewire.” Here “escaping” means crossing a block boundary, not escaping to another function or heap object.

blocks.text: An operation can have an effect without producing a value

Instructions do different jobs. add computes a result that later instructions can consume. store changes memory but supplies no result value. ret ends a function invocation; a call can either return a value or be void. These effects matter, even when the operation has no result.

Our current question is narrow: which instruction results need a different way to reach another block? A void-result instruction has no such result to spill. Filtering it out means “leave this operation out of the value worklist,” not “delete the operation” or “ignore its side effects.” We will handle branch terminators separately when changing control flow.

rows: Keep the effect; do not demote a nonexistent result.
Needs the separate storage filter in the next lesson.

blocks.text: Why the storage itself is a different kind of result

The demotion strategy gives a value a storage slot, writes its value into that slot, and loads it where needed. alloca creates the slot and returns its address. That address naturally appears in stores and loads in several blocks, so a generic “used outside its block” test would select the allocation too.

For this preparation algorithm, storage pointers are the stable foundation we rely on. Adding another slot just to transport the address of the first slot is not the intended repair. We exclude AllocaInst from the ordinary value worklist and require supported storage allocations to remain in the original entry, where they dominate all the later memory accesses.

Skipping an alloca is not proof that every allocation is safe. A non-entry alloca might be bypassed by a new edge; a variable-sized or repeated allocation may have meaningful execution/lifetime behavior. The stricter eligibility lesson rejects those cases before full rewriting. A normal entry slot is allocated once per function invocation, not once for the whole program.

blocks.text: What ordinary-value demotion preserves

For an ordinary instruction, the calculation is already in the right block. The problem is how a later block obtains its result. DemoteRegToStack keeps the defining calculation, stores its result into entry-allocated storage, and supplies loads for uses. The direct SSA connection across blocks becomes explicit communication through memory.

Before: calculate %sum ─────────────→ another block uses %sum
After:  calculate %sum → store slot → another block loads slot → uses load

The name “Reg” refers to LLVM’s register-like SSA results, not a physical CPU register we are choosing. This step can add instructions; it is preparation for changing the graph, not a speed optimization.

Memory transport does not make arbitrary execution orders correct. The final state machine must still arrange for the appropriate store to execute before its corresponding load, preserving the original computation’s behavior. Preparation makes the IR representation suitable for that later rewrite; it does not prove the rewrite correct.

blocks.text: A PHI carries a choice, not just one calculation

Ordinary-value demotion moves the result of one defining calculation through memory. PHI demotion has a different source of truth: the executed incoming path decides which of several incoming values should be carried. Preserving a PHI therefore requires preserving the path/value association.

condition=true  → left  → choose 10 → join returns 10
condition=false → right → choose 20 → join returns 20

In the demoted diamond, each chosen path writes its own incoming value and join reads the slot. Writing both 10 and 20 unconditionally before join would always leave the last write; allocating a slot without the path-specific writes would not encode any choice. The memory operations are a replacement for the PHI’s meaning, not merely a way to make the PHI instruction disappear.

Loops use the same abstraction to choose an initial value on entry and a carried value on later iterations. More complex edges and interacting PHIs make placement subtle. The hand trace below explains this diamond; the LLVM utility is responsible for the general mechanics used by the prototype.

blocks.text: Why blocks become states

An original branch names its next block directly. A shared dispatcher needs a value it can inspect to choose that next block. A state ID is our encoding of the next block’s identity: store a number, reach dispatch, and let its switch decode the number back to a destination.

Original intention: run left next.
Encoded intention:  next state = 0.
Dispatcher rule:    state 0 means left.

The numbers have no intrinsic meaning. Any unique, consistently used assignment would work. Mapping the prepared blocks in function order gives us deterministic dumps and a simple table to inspect. Mapping after demotion also includes any blocks introduced during preparation.

The original entry is setup rather than a recurring state: its allocations must execute once per invocation, and the entry block cannot acquire predecessors. Excluding it keeps dispatcher cycles from re-entering setup. We assign IDs before appending dispatch/invalid so the machine’s own machinery does not accidentally become an original program state.
Task: After both demotion stages, map the original non-entry blocks to unsigned state IDs. Do not create dispatcher blocks during this traversal.
Before you begin — what a state represents

A state number identifies which original block the future dispatcher should run next. It is not an instruction count, a block name, or a new block. In this design, entry stays setup and is excluded from the switch’s ordinary state cases.
The template to start with
Step 1 — Include the map type
#include "llvm/ADT/DenseMap.h"
DenseMap maps a key to a value. Here the key is BasicBlock* and the value is unsigned. The vector keeps the order; the map supports looking up a destination’s ID when rewriting a branch.
Step 2 — Keep setup out of the state loop

if (&BB == entry)
    continue;

The entry block must execute once, particularly its stack allocations. Dispatching through setup repeatedly could allocate storage or repeat initialization on each transition. The pointer returned by &F.getEntryBlock() identifies the actual entry regardless of its name.
Step 3 — Record a block and its ID
Take the address because BB is a reference to the block. The next lesson revisits the pointer and pair-construction errors found in the first draft.
Step 4 — Print in vector order
Iterate stateBlocks to print deterministic output. DenseMap iteration order is not a stable display order. Do not rely on LLVM block names as unique persistent IDs.

blocks.text: What the dispatcher adds to the program

A dispatcher is a shared decision block. Instead of every original branch choosing another program block directly, each rewritten transition will write the desired state and jump to this block. The dispatcher reads the state and uses its switch to choose the corresponding original block.

entry setup → [write next state] → dispatch
                                  read state
                                  switch 0 → left
                                         1 → right
                                         2 → join

We use one i32 memory slot because many different blocks must update the same next-state information. A single SSA name cannot be repeatedly assigned by all those transitions. Its alloca lives in entry so the address is available everywhere; the stored contents change as execution moves between states. An alternative design could maintain SSA PHIs for state, but this course chooses memory so we do not have to repair those PHIs while restructuring the graph.

This lesson deliberately constructs complete but disconnected machinery. It separates “can we build a valid load/switch/case structure?” from “have we redirected execution correctly?” An unreachable dispatcher does not demonstrate flattening yet, and its uninitialized slot must not be read on a live path. The next connection lesson supplies the first write before making it reachable.

The invalid default expresses the invariant that our own transitions store only mapped state IDs. Ending it with unreachable makes that assumption explicit to LLVM; it is not a safe fallback if the assumption is broken.
Task: After state mapping, add an i32 state slot and two complete new blocks. Preserve the old branch structure at this construction checkpoint.
The template to start with
Step 1 — Choose an insertion point

IRBuilder is a helper for inserting instructions. getFirstInsertionPt() returns an iterator to the first legal insertion position; * obtains the instruction and & takes its address. The builder inserts before that instruction. This expression differs from &*dispatcher, which just recovers a pointer you already had.
Step 2 — Allocate the state once
auto *stateSlot = setup.CreateAlloca(setup.getInt32Ty(), nullptr, "ms.state");

getInt32Ty() returns the LLVM i32 type. CreateAlloca returns the storage pointer. nullptr supplies no array-size operand, meaning the default single element in this overload. The final string is the IR result name. No store is added yet because the dispatcher is deliberately unreachable.
Step 3 — Append the two blocks

LLVMContext owns shared IR context such as uniqued types. &F attaches each block to this function. With no insertion-before argument, the blocks are appended; the original entry remains first. stateBlocks was collected before creation, so neither new block receives a normal state ID.
Step 4 — Terminate the invalid-state path

llvm::IRBuilder<> invalidBuilder(invalidBlock);
invalidBuilder.CreateUnreachable();

unreachable ends the block and declares that this path must never execute in a valid run. It is not a runtime exception handler or a recovery return. Correct state writes must prevent invalid values from selecting it.
Step 5 — Load and switch
CreateLoad needs the loaded value type and pointer. CreateSwitch creates the terminator and sets its default destination. Its third argument reserves case capacity; it does not add case edges.
Step 6 — Populate the cases and mark the mutation

getInt32(ID) creates an i32 integer constant, unlike getInt32Ty(), which supplies a Type*. Keep changed declared before construction so the final preservation result includes the new instructions and blocks.
The full construction stage

Place this after the demotion and state-mapping stages. It replaces the old final preservation return. The variable entry is the BasicBlock* saved during mapping; if your source calls it entry_ptr, use that spelling consistently.

  -S tests/ir/phi.ll -o build/phi-dispatcher.ll

blocks.text: A block has an identity, a label, and an ending

Three different ideas appear when we create a block. The C++ variable lets the pass refer to the block object. The IR name makes printed output readable. The block’s instructions and final terminator determine what the generated program actually does. Spelling a block ms.dispatch does not give it dispatcher behavior.

Likewise, naming a block invalid does not make it an exception handler or give it an implicit exit. LLVM requires a terminator even in a currently unreachable block. The default case needs a defined IR structure that accurately states our invariant, rather than an empty block that merely has a plausible label.

A dot is member access in C++, not part of an identifier. Writing ms.dispatch makes the parser look for a member named dispatch on an object named ms. Use dispatcher as the variable name.

BasicBlock::Create returns BasicBlock*. The function owns the attached block. Do not try to construct a local BasicBlock value from that pointer or take the address of an invented local object.

auto *dispatcher = llvm::BasicBlock::Create(
    F.getContext(), "ms.dispatch", &F);

The placeholder name in the teaching signature meant “supply a name here”; it was not a predefined variable. Quoted "ms.dispatch" is the block’s display name and may contain a dot even though the C++ identifier cannot.

After the declaration errors are fixed, an empty invalid block would still fail LLVM verification. Compilation checks C++ syntax and types; verify checks the IR your C++ creates.

blocks.text: Why the first state must come from the old entry edge

The dispatcher exists, but the original entry still follows its old branch. To make execution use the new route, we must translate that branch’s intention into a stored state ID, then send control to dispatch. For loop.ll, the old destination is header, so the first stored state must decode to header.

After:  entry → store ID(header) → dispatch → header

The order is essential: dispatch loads the slot, so entry must write it first. A universal store of zero would be correct only if the actual destination happened to have ID zero. We read the destination and consult the map because the mapping, not the numeric spelling, defines the meaning.

This first connection handles an unconditional branch: there is one intended successor. It leaves header/body loop edges direct, so it demonstrates only the first dispatcher hop. A conditional entry needs to encode a choice, and full flattening must translate the other original transitions as well.

lessons.summary: Tighten the Day 1 guard before turning the prototype into a complete dispatcher. Scope is a correctness decision.
lessons.takeaway: Reject unsupported input before the first edit.

blocks.text: Why a transformation needs a support contract

A read-only pass can inspect instructions without taking responsibility for new execution paths. A transformation has a stronger obligation: every accepted case must still mean the same thing after our edits. The fact that LLVM accepts an input does not mean this particular algorithm knows how to transform it.

For example, an allocation in a later block may be valid in the original graph because every use follows that block. Dispatching directly to a use can bypass the allocation. Simply skipping alloca during value collection does not repair that relationship. Other constructs have special calling, exception, or value-type rules that our simple rewrite does not maintain.

Preflight makes these assumptions executable: unsupported input is rejected before the first edit. This keeps a rejected function intact instead of leaving it half-demoted or half-rewired. A narrow accepted subset is a deliberate semantic boundary, not a claim that rejected LLVM features are generally invalid.
Task: Future exercise: expand FunctionEligibility before enabling the complete rewrite below. These chapters are a book draft; your working implementation has not been updated for you.
Why the old guard is not enough

The earlier guard supported inspection and a limited prototype. A new dispatcher edge can bypass a non-entry alloca, making its pointer fail dominance. Some LLVM instruction results cannot be spilled as ordinary scalars. Special call semantics can forbid the control-flow changes we are proposing.
The template to start with
Step 1 — State a narrow contract

This teaching implementation accepts valid, ordinary scalar LLVM IR: integers, floating-point values, pointers, supported branch terminators, and static entry allocations. It is conservative. It rejects explicit intrinsic calls for now rather than assuming every llvm.* operation is safe. This is narrower than “all C++ functions.”
Step 2 — Reject non-static allocation

isStaticAlloca() encodes LLVM’s entry/constant-size rule, including restrictions such as inalloca. Do not simply move a loop’s alloca into entry: changing how often storage is allocated may change behavior.
Step 3 — Reject exceptional result and call forms

The full reference rejects non-scalar instruction results, naked functions, inline assembly calls, convergent calls, operand bundles, returns_twice, musttail, and intrinsic calls. Explain the reason for each before relaxing it; rejection is a defined limitation, not a bug to hide.
Study-session walkthrough — operation, result, and storage are different

These are the smaller steps used in our live lesson. Write each guard inside the existing instruction loop in FunctionEligibility::check, then test it before adding the next. Eligibility inspects the original IR without changing it; the flattening pass must call it before demotion.

%sum = add i32 %x, 1
%slot = alloca i32
store i32 %sum, ptr %slot
%loaded = load i32, ptr %slot

This is an illustrative instruction fragment, not a complete function. add computes a 32-bit integer. alloca reserves storage for an i32 but produces a pointer to that storage. store writes an integer through the pointer and produces no result. load reads an integer through the pointer and defines a new i32 result. The memory contents can change, although each named SSA instruction result still has one static definition.

blocks.text: Do not confuse I.getType() with the allocated element type. For %slot = alloca i32, I.getType() is ptr. Integer arithmetic and an integer load can both produce i32 while being different operations.
Study-session walkthrough — why an allocation must dominate its uses

define i32 @nonentry_alloca() {
entry:
  br label %allocate
allocate:
  %slot = alloca i32
  store i32 7, ptr %slot
  br label %read
read:
  %value = load i32, ptr %slot
  ret i32 %value
}

define starts a function returning i32; the empty parentheses mean no arguments. Each colon starts a basic block. br label %allocate transfers execution to that block. %slot names the address returned by alloca; store i32 7, ptr %slot writes 7 into that address. The next branch reaches read, where load reads the stored integer. ret returns it, so the original program returns 7.

Originally every route to read passes through allocate. Dispatcher edges can create a route to read that bypasses allocate, so the pointer definition no longer dominates its use. Excluding allocations from the ordinary value-demotion worklist does not repair this relationship. Our prototype rejects allocations that are not supported static entry allocations.

dyn_cast returns a typed pointer to the existing instruction, or nullptr for another instruction class. isStaticAlloca checks LLVM’s static-entry allocation classification; it is not merely a test for the word alloca. Entry storage executes once per function invocation. Hoisting arbitrary allocations yourself could change allocation frequency or lifetime, so rejection is the current policy.
Study-session walkthrough — build the result-type guard

LLVM supports more value types than this prototype promises to transform. We deliberately accept ordinary integer, floating-point, and pointer results, plus operations with no result. This is a conservative support boundary, not a claim that LLVM cannot store structures or vectors.

Each method returns a C++ bool. The || operators mean any one category is allowed; !supported means no category matched. const auto * borrows the LLVM Type object without allowing mutation through that pointer. This is compiler-side inspection, not a target-program instruction.

blocks.text: Eligibility and worklist filtering answer different questions. A void store is an allowed operation, so eligibility accepts it. During ordinary value demotion we skip it because there is no produced value to spill. Rejecting every void result would incorrectly reject stores, branches, and returns.

The braces { i32, i32 } describe a structure with two integer fields, not a control-flow block. zeroinitializer supplies zero for both fields. insertvalue creates a new aggregate with field 0 replaced by x; extractvalue reads field 0 from that aggregate, without a pointer or memory load. The original function returns x. Our guard rejects %pair because the result is a structure, even though %first and the function’s return type are i32.
Study-session walkthrough — an intrinsic is a special operation expressed as a call

An LLVM intrinsic has semantics defined by LLVM rather than an ordinary user-supplied function body. Many are represented with call instructions naming llvm.* functions. The call is the instruction; the intrinsic identifies the operation it invokes. Intrinsics can describe arithmetic, memory, lifetime, coroutine, and other operations with different constraints.

declare supplies a signature without a body. @llvm.ctpop.i32 is a module-level name for the intrinsic that counts set bits in an i32. define starts our ordinary wrapper function. Its i32 %x argument is supplied by a caller; call passes that value to the intrinsic and binds the returned i32 to %count. ret returns that result. For x = 7, binary 111, the answer is 3.

A scalar result does not establish that every operation is supported by our control-flow rewrite. We reject explicit intrinsic calls conservatively until their individual semantics are covered. This does not mean every intrinsic is unsafe. The ordinary recursive call in recursion.ll remains outside this blanket intrinsic restriction.

Keep the specific coroutine diagnostic first, then reject the other intrinsic calls. This incremental version uses IntrinsicInst; the full reference below recognizes intrinsic callees within its broader CallBase checks. Both implement the conservative policy, while the full version also checks other special call forms.
Study-session walkthrough — musttail is a requirement, not a hint

Here @callee is an ordinary declared function, not an intrinsic. musttail modifies the call and requires a tail-call transfer under LLVM’s rules. The function returns its result immediately. This is a stronger contract than an ordinary call that can return to surrounding code and continue doing work.

The required call/return relationship constrains the instructions permitted between them, with limited exceptions in LLVM’s rules. A generic spill or CFG rewrite must not insert arbitrary work there. Our prototype rejects musttail before any edit instead of promising to preserve those constraints. The unchanged example is valid; the rejection is about the transformation’s scope.

CallInst recognizes the call instruction class; isMustTailCall asks whether this particular call carries the mandatory marker. An ordinary call passes this check. This is separate from the intrinsic check because an ordinary function can be the target of a musttail call.

blocks.text: Demoting arithmetic removes direct cross-block data uses, but the alloca result is itself an SSA pointer. blocks.title: Why special call semantics constrain CFG rewriting

blocks.text: An ordinary call is not the whole story. musttail requires strict call/return structure; inserting a spill reload or transition between the call and return can violate its contract. returns_twice marks calls that can return more than once, so an apparently single forward path does not capture their control effects. A convergent operation has additional constraints on how control flow may be transformed around participating operations. Operand bundles carry semantic information beyond ordinary operands, such as deoptimization or funclet context.

blocks.text: Why separate the builder from the pass

The transformation now has three distinct questions: may we edit this function, have its values been prepared, and how do we construct the new graph? Mixing all three in one long run() makes it harder to identify which assumption a failure violates.

StateMachineBuilder gives graph construction one boundary. Its input is a valid, accepted, prepared function; its job is to translate that function’s control flow. This separation lets us test a prepared graph directly while keeping rejection and preparation in the orchestration pass.

A precondition is an obligation on the caller, not an automatic check performed by a C++ class. Extracting the code does not make unsafe input safe. Naming those obligations is what lets another reader understand when this helper may be used.

An original conditional branch answers “which block next?” from an i1 condition. We want the same runtime decision to survive, but with both paths first going through dispatch. Replace the edge choice with a value choice: select the true destination’s state ID when the condition is true, otherwise the false destination’s ID.

Both select alternatives here are state constants. We are not moving the side effects of both original paths into one block; dispatch still executes only the selected destination. blocks.text: A switch still needs its complete decision rule

A source switch can have several named cases and a default for every other value. Flattening must preserve that entire mapping. We encode the original outcome as a next-state value instead of letting the old switch transfer control directly.

Start: next = ID(default destination).
For case value k: if input == k, choose ID(case destination).
Finally: store next and go to dispatch.

Starting from the default is what preserves unmatched inputs. Comparing every case to the same original condition preserves the case decisions; valid case values are distinct, although multiple values may share one destination. The condition’s integer type can differ from the i32 type chosen for state IDs.

There are now two different switches in the story. The original switch represents a program decision that this lesson translates into comparisons and selects. The new dispatcher switch decodes the state ID and must remain in place. Confusing the two can make the transformer rewrite its own routing machinery.

The switch’s integer condition is not necessarily i32. Its case constants already have the matching type. The generated comparison yields i1, while destination state constants remain i32.

next = b.CreateSelect(matches, stateOf(oneCase.getCaseSuccessor()), next, "ms.next");

lessons.summary: Combine the branch forms into one complete, carefully bounded state-machine builder.

blocks.text: Full flattening is a repeated protocol, not just a new switch

Creating a dispatcher and connecting entry changes only one hop. The complete machine requires each original non-terminal transition to follow the same protocol: compute the intended next state, store it, then branch to dispatch. The switch chooses the next block, whose own transition repeats that process.

setup → choose/store state → dispatch → original block
                               ↑              |
                               └─ store next ─┘
An original return finishes the invocation instead of taking the loop back.

This is the key behavioral invariant: at each dispatcher visit, the slot encodes exactly the destination the original program would have chosen at that transition. A valid number is not enough; it must be the correct number for the original condition and path.

Snapshot original terminators before appending new blocks so the rewrite applies only to the old program’s transitions. Keep ret and unreachable terminal rather than manufacturing another state after they have already ended a path. The shared store/branch tail is appropriate only when a next state exists.

lessons.title: Orchestrate policy, preparation, and construction
lessons.summary: Finish the pass as an ordered pipeline and account for every mutation in analysis invalidation.
lessons.takeaway: One pass coordinates; each helper has a focused job.

blocks.text: Why the order of phases is part of correctness

The pass is now a pipeline within a pipeline. Eligibility protects the input boundary; preparation changes how values travel; construction changes how blocks are reached; preservation reporting tells later passes which cached facts remain usable. Each phase establishes assumptions needed by the next.

reject unsupported input before edits
    ↓
prepare values for a different graph
    ↓
translate control-flow decisions into states
    ↓
report whether cached analyses became stale

Reordering these calls is not just a style change. Rewiring first can leave old PHIs and SSA uses invalid. Rejecting last leaves unsupported functions mutated. Reporting no change after demotion lets later passes reuse obsolete results. Track all phases’ changes without accidentally skipping a phase whose call has side effects.

The template to start with
Step 1 — Keep rejection before modification
No demotion or state allocation should precede the decision. Rejection after a partial transformation violates the unchanged-input contract.
Step 2 — Combine change information without skipping work

bool changed = !phis.empty() || !escaping.empty();
changed |= StateMachineBuilder::build(F);

Here |= is boolean accumulation that evaluates the builder call even if changed was already true. Writing changed = changed || build(F) would short-circuit and skip construction whenever demotion changed the function. Alternatively call build first into a separate bool, then combine the results.
Step 3 — Preserve conservatively

Return none() after any mutation in this teaching implementation. Preserving a particular analysis is a claim you must justify and, for dependent cached analyses, implement correctly. “The graph still looks similar” is not enough.

lessons.originalTitle: Inspect the final shape with LLVM tools
lessons.summary: Learn to diagnose a transformation from IR, pass traces, and verifier errors before relying on runtime comparisons.
lessons.takeaway: The verifier catches structure; inspection explains how it was built.

blocks.text: What inspecting the final graph can establish

A compiler transformation has two separate obligations: produce well-formed IR and preserve intended behavior. Structural inspection addresses the first and checks our design invariants. We want to see a live entry-to-dispatch path, valid state storage, the intended cases, and the rewritten transitions.

The mere presence of a switch or a block named ms.dispatch is weak evidence: it might be unreachable while the original graph still runs unchanged. Follow actual successors from entry and verify the relations among blocks. LLVM’s verifier also checks rules such as types, terminators, and dominance; it does not prove our state IDs choose the right answers.

This is why the next lesson compares executions. A true/false ID swap can be structurally legal yet wrong. Keep structural checks and behavioral checks as complementary tests rather than expecting one to replace the other.
Task: Future exercise: establish structural evidence for the complete rewrite before measuring performance.
The template to start with

opt -load-pass-plugin="$PWD/build/libMiniShield.so" \
  -passes='function(minishield-flatten),verify' \
  -S tests/ir/loop.ll -o build/loop-flat.ll
# TODO: inspect setup, dispatch, state stores, and terminal paths.
Step 1 — Inspect invariants, not exact names

LLVM may uniquify names such as ms.dispatch. Use opcode/edge relationships for assertions. Text dumps remain useful for understanding, but a test that only greps for a name can pass with a dead or malformed intended structure.
Step 2 — Read an SSA dominance error

If a definition no longer dominates a use, locate both blocks and draw the new incoming edges. Do not hide the error by deleting verify. Check that a slot was allocated in preserved entry and that the use refers to a local reload, not an old cross-block definition.
Step 3 — Trace passes

opt -load-pass-plugin="$PWD/build/libMiniShield.so" \
  -passes='function(minishield-flatten),verify' \
  -debug-pass-manager -disable-output tests/ir/loop.ll
Use the pass-manager trace to distinguish “loaded,” “scheduled,” “skipped,” and “ran.” Optional passes can be skipped on optnone functions; a missing diagnostic is not always a broken plugin.
Step 4 — Preserve a failing artifact
Keep the smallest failing input, the command, the compiler version, and stderr. Save generated IR under build/. Record which stage first breaks rather than changing several phases at once.

State allocation dominates every load/store using its pointer.
Every generated block has a terminator.
Dispatch cases reference the intended state blocks.
Original state transitions store a valid ID before dispatch.
The default invalid path must be unreachable under valid state transitions.

Reserve storage for the shown element type in this function invocation and produce its address, not the stored integer. `alloca i32` reserves one i32 slot. The allocation does not initialize its contents; a store must supply a value before an intended read.

`br label %B` always transfers control to block B. `br i1 %C, label %A, label %B` goes to A for true and B for false; their order matters. A branch is the block’s final instruction and produces no result. It does not execute both destinations.

Read a value from memory: in `load i32, ptr %slot`, i32 is the loaded value’s type and %slot is its address. The left-hand result gets the current contents, not another copy of the address. Define one value by the edge just used to enter this block. Each `[ VALUE, %PREDECESSOR ]` pairs an incoming value with its source block; it is not an array access. lessons.title: Compare observable behavior on a defined domain
lessons.originalTitle: Compare observable behavior on a defined domain
lessons.summary: Build original and transformed functions from the same front-end IR, then compare outputs for bounded inputs.
lessons.takeaway: Equivalent behavior is stronger than valid IR, but testing is still finite evidence.

blocks.text: Why valid IR is not enough

Imagine a rewrite that reverses the destinations of a conditional branch. The result can have correct types, terminators, and dominance, but return the wrong discount. To test meaning, run the original and protected versions on the same inputs and compare what a caller can observe.

This is differential testing: one implementation is the reference for the other. Our small driver exposes a numeric result on stdout and an exit status. The test domain must use defined arithmetic and valid arguments; otherwise a disagreement might come from a broken fixture rather than our transformation.

We compile one common input IR and vary whether MiniShield transforms it. Keeping the driver, compiler settings, and final optimization the same helps isolate that difference. Finite tests give evidence for the tested cases, not proof for all inputs. Also inspect the graph: a stub that does nothing can pass every output comparison.
Task: Future exercise: write a C input function and a separate driver. Transform the function’s IR, not the driver that parses arguments and prints results.
The template to start with
Step 1 — Bound the test domain

Use amounts from -1000 through 10000 and levels 0 through 5. The arithmetic below cannot overflow int on that domain. Comparing two programs that both have source undefined behavior is not a meaningful correctness test.
Step 2 — Write the function and driver
Save that as tests/cases/discount.c and the following as tests/cases/discount_driver.c. The command-line guard keeps executions inside the documented domain.
Step 3 — Create one common IR input

The front end emits unoptimized IR without the O0 optnone attribute so the optional pass will run. Both variants then use the same -O2 backend. This separates the tested transformation from accidental differences in front-end settings.

mkdir -p build/differential
clang -O0 -Xclang -disable-O0-optnone -S -emit-llvm \
  tests/cases/discount.c -o build/differential/common.ll
opt -load-pass-plugin="$PWD/build/libMiniShield.so" \
  -passes='function(minishield-flatten),verify' \
  -S build/differential/common.ll -o build/differential/protected.ll
clang -O2 tests/cases/discount_driver.c build/differential/common.ll \
  -o build/differential/original
clang -O2 tests/cases/discount_driver.c build/differential/protected.ll \
  -o build/differential/protected
Step 4 — Compare boundary and representative inputs

build/differential/original 1000 2
build/differential/protected 1000 2
# Expected stdout from each: 900
build/differential/original -1 0
build/differential/protected -1 0
# Expected stdout from each: 0

items: Same common input IR, driver, backend flags, toolchain, and inputs.
Both processes exit normally; compare exit status and stdout. Treat crashes/timeouts as failures.
Inspect transformed IR to ensure a transformation actually happened; equality is trivial if the pass skipped everything.
Passing examples provide evidence for this test domain, not a universal proof.

blocks.text: Why a simple diamond is not a sufficient test corpus

A diamond exercises one merge and two paths. It does not exercise a loop’s repeated value choices, two PHIs that depend on each other, a switch’s default, several returns, or an edge that needs special placement during demotion. A transformer can handle the first example perfectly and still break on these different relationships.

Choose each new fixture to stress one assumption. An initial/loop-carried value tests first versus later iterations. Shared switch destinations test whether values and destinations were confused. Parallel PHIs test whether old values are preserved before any replacement overwrites them.

The goal is not simply more lines of IR. Small focused fixtures let you predict the graph and results independently, recognize a specific failure, and keep a regression that explains the bug. Unsupported cases need equally deliberate rejection tests rather than being silently omitted.
Task: Future exercise: grow the fixture corpus before claiming the transformer handles general control flow.
The template to start with
Step 1 — Test parallel PHI selection

Two loop PHIs can exchange old values. Their incoming values are conceptually selected together. A naive hand-written sequence of stores and loads can overwrite an old value before the other PHI uses it; do not replace LLVM’s helper with that shortcut.

rows: Meaning and operand order in these listings

Add the two same-typed operands and define the sum. In these unflagged i32 examples, arithmetic is modulo 2^32; the test inputs stay in the small intended range. This calculates data, such as the next loop counter or x + 1, rather than choosing a block.

Reserve storage for the shown element type in this function invocation and produce its address, not the stored integer. `alloca i32` reserves one i32 slot. The allocation does not initialize its contents; a store must supply a value before an intended read.

`br label %B` always transfers control to block B. `br i1 %C, label %A, label %B` goes to A for true and B for false; their order matters. A branch is the block’s final instruction and produces no result. It does not execute both destinations.

Compare two same-typed integers and produce i1, which can feed br or select. `slt` asks whether the left operand is smaller using signed integer interpretation, so a negative i32 is below zero. The comparison computes a condition; it does not jump by itself.

Read left-to-right: compare the first integer operand with the second, then use the resulting i1 as a condition. For the loop it compares the current counter with the bound; for the discount kernel it checks whether the amount is negative.

Read a value from memory: in `load i32, ptr %slot`, i32 is the loaded value’s type and %slot is its address. The left-hand result gets the current contents, not another copy of the address. Each load defines a new SSA value; it does not compute the value that a missing earlier store should have supplied.

Define one value by the edge just used to enter this block. Each `[ VALUE, %PREDECESSOR ]` pairs an incoming value with its source block; it is not an array access. The PHI’s i32 type applies to every incoming value, so a literal inside a bracket does not repeat the type. PHIs go at the start of a block. On a loop’s first entry choose its entry value, and on a back edge choose its carried value. Multiple PHIs select incoming values together, rather than sequentially overwriting each other.

End this function invocation and return the typed operand to its caller. `ret i32 %v` returns the integer value, while `ret ptr ...` returns a pointer. A return does not proceed to the next printed block or automatically go back to dispatch.

Produce a value from `select i1 CONDITION, TYPE TRUE_VALUE, TYPE FALSE_VALUE`. A true condition chooses the first alternative, false the second; alternatives have the same type. This does not branch or conditionally execute the instructions that computed the operands. Here the chosen result is either a destination’s state number or the final return value.

Write memory: in `store i32 VALUE, ptr ADDRESS`, the first operand is the value and the second is the destination address. A store has an effect but no result name. Writing a state slot changes the next routing choice; writing a demotion slot transports an original program value.

Subtract the second operand from the first and define the difference. Operand order matters: a − b is not b − a. In the discount kernel it removes the computed discount; in the swap loop it makes the current ordering observable.

Transfer control according to one integer value. The destination immediately after the condition is the default for no matching case. Each line inside `[...]` pairs a typed case constant with `label %DESTINATION`; only one destination is taken. An original switch chooses a program outcome; a dispatcher switch decodes the stored state ID. The brackets are a case list, not a runtime array.

End the block by asserting that execution never reaches this point on a defined run. Actually executing it is undefined behavior; it is not error recovery, a return, or a C++ exception. The state-machine invariant must prevent a bad stored ID from taking this default path.

lessons.title: Account for optimizers, debug data, and limitations
lessons.originalTitle: Account for optimizers, debug data, and limitations
lessons.summary: Understand where the transformation sits in a compilation pipeline and what the prototype does not guarantee.
lessons.takeaway: Measure the artifact you actually ship, not the intermediate picture you like.

blocks.text: The pass is one stage in a larger compiler

The IR we print immediately after flattening is not necessarily the code that ships. Later optimizations can remove redundant loads, simplify state choices, restructure loops, or eliminate some dispatcher machinery. Earlier optimization can introduce forms outside our prototype’s support contract.

We therefore need two kinds of observation: does the complete pipeline preserve results, and does the final artifact still have the structure we intend to study? A fast, correct executable may no longer demonstrate flattening if optimization simplified it away.

Debug locations and branch-weight metadata also describe program relationships. New instructions and edges do not automatically inherit all the old relationships correctly. Documenting what we preserve, reject, or leave unsupported keeps the technical claim aligned with the actual implementation.
Task: Future exercise: record the transformation’s placement relative to optimization and inspect both intermediate and final artifacts.
The template to start with

common IR → [optional optimization] → MiniShield → [backend optimization] → executable
# TODO: choose and record the exact pipeline for each experiment.
Step 1 — Expect simplification

An optimizer can simplify state dispatch or replace a branch-heavy function with straight-line code. A successful build or matching output does not prove that a dispatcher remains in the emitted binary. Inspect optimized IR and disassembly; report when a candidate fixture no longer demonstrates flattening.
Step 2 — Keep comparisons fair

Hold source, compiler, target, optimization level, driver, and input domain constant when comparing original and protected variants. Changing the transformation stage is an experiment to label, not an invisible adjustment to improve a result.
Step 3 — Treat metadata by meaning

Set the builder’s debug location from the original terminator for new transition instructions. Do not blindly copy branch-weight metadata to edges with a different meaning. The prototype does not promise fully preserved debug-variable locations or profile quality.
Step 4 — Describe invalid-state behavior accurately

The unreachable default is an internal invariant, not input validation. Loading an uninitialized state is not automatically zero, and executing unreachable is undefined behavior. A real robustness feature would require deliberate initialization and a defined failure policy, separately designed and tested.
The full limitations note to adapt

Prototype scope: ordinary scalar valid IR and static entry allocas.
Rejected: EH/personality, coroutines, block addresses, unsupported terminators,
          special call forms, explicit intrinsics, non-static allocas,
          non-scalar instruction results, and naked functions.
Not promised: formal behavior proof, arbitrary C++ support, anti-reversing
              guarantees, unchanged debug/profile quality, or immunity to
              later optimization simplifying the dispatcher.
Verify

Compare pre- and post-optimization IR for at least one fixture. Confirm the reported size/runtime refer to the final executable under the stated pipeline. Record both supported and rejected function counts.

lessons.takeaway: A checklist is a claim only after its evidence exists.

blocks.text: What finishing Day 2 should mean

Reaching the last line of a builder is not the same as establishing a working transformation. We need an accepted-input boundary, correctly transported values, faithful state transitions, valid output IR, and tested behavior. The checklist turns those broad goals into evidence we can inspect.

Keep three states separate: a chapter is written, you have implemented its exercise, and its behavior has been checked. A full reference in the book establishes the first; it does not automatically establish the other two in your working tree. Day 3 makes the checks repeatable and measures the resulting artifacts.
Task: Future exercise: review the implementation and evidence before beginning Day 3. The chapters describe work to do; they do not mark it done for you.
The template to start with

[ ] Strict preflight rejects unsupported input before edits.
[ ] PHIs and suitable escaping values are prepared.
[ ] Entry is preserved as one-time setup.
[ ] Conditional/unconditional/switch transitions choose correct states.
[ ] Returns and unreachable remain terminal.
[ ] verify succeeds on the complete fixture set.
[ ] Accepted fixtures match original behavior on the defined test domain.
[ ] Rejected fixtures have intended reasons and unchanged canonical IR.
[ ] Limitations and optimizer placement are documented.
Step 1 — Name the unfinished item
If any box lacks evidence, keep it open and identify a smallest failing fixture or missing test. “The code compiles” does not fill the behavior boxes.
Step 2 — Save only source and reproducible fixtures

Commit the code, build configuration, documentation, and intentional test inputs. Keep build products and before/after generated IR in build/. The local table script remains excluded unless you explicitly decide to track it later.
Step 3 — Move into test infrastructure

Day 3 turns manual observations into repeatable unit, integration, and differential checks, then measures final artifacts. It adds evidence rather than assuming that many successful printouts are a test suite.

Reading this LLVM program from zero

Do not read every displayed block as one straight-line script. A call supplies the function inputs and starts its first block. Within the selected block, follow the written instructions until a terminator chooses another block or returns to the caller. A label names a block; it does not execute an operation by itself.

rows: `define` starts a function body. `@count_to` is the module-level function name; `i32` immediately before it is the return type. Parentheses contain typed inputs supplied by the caller; braces contain its blocks.

i1 means one bit: 0 is false and 1 is true for a condition; i32 means a 32-bit integer bit pattern; signed interpretation comes from operations such as slt or sdiv, not from a separate signed i32 type.

An opaque pointer value: it can represent an address or the special handle returned in the coroutine example. It does not contain an i32 integer or encode a pointee type. A load/store spells out the type of value accessed separately from the pointer.

The left side names the result of this instruction. Each SSA result has one static defining instruction; input arguments are values supplied at function entry. A name is a handle for a value, not a mutable source variable or a guaranteed CPU register.

The colon defines a block label; the label operand names a jump destination. `%` is also used for local result/argument names, so use the type/context to distinguish a value from a block target. `@` instead identifies a module-level symbol.

This is a typed literal: the i-prefixed part specifies the bit width, and the decimal part is the constant value. For example, a case number or stored state ID is an integer value, unlike a `%name` or `name:` label.

Everything after a semicolon on that line is a comment for the reader. The printer lists incoming blocks after preds; it is not an instruction, an execution order, or a separate edge definition. Branch/switch operands actually define the edges.

Alignment is in bytes, not elements, bits, or a value to store. An aligned alloca provides suitably aligned storage; an aligned load/store promises that its pointer meets that alignment. It does not initialize memory or change the integer read/written.

rows: Meaning and operand order in these listings

Add the two same-typed operands and define the sum. In these unflagged i32 examples, arithmetic is modulo 2^32; the test inputs stay in the small intended range. This calculates data, such as the next loop counter or x + 1, rather than choosing a block.

Reserve storage for the shown element type in this function invocation and produce its address, not the stored integer. `alloca i32` reserves one i32 slot. The allocation does not initialize its contents; a store must supply a value before an intended read.

`br label %B` always transfers control to block B. `br i1 %C, label %A, label %B` goes to A for true and B for false; their order matters. A branch is the block’s final instruction and produces no result. It does not execute both destinations.

Compare two same-typed integers and produce i1, which can feed br or select. `slt` asks whether the left operand is smaller using signed integer interpretation, so a negative i32 is below zero. The comparison computes a condition; it does not jump by itself.

Read left-to-right: compare the first integer operand with the second, then use the resulting i1 as a condition. For the loop it compares the current counter with the bound; for the discount kernel it checks whether the amount is negative.

Read a value from memory: in `load i32, ptr %slot`, i32 is the loaded value’s type and %slot is its address. The left-hand result gets the current contents, not another copy of the address. Each load defines a new SSA value; it does not compute the value that a missing earlier store should have supplied.

Define one value by the edge just used to enter this block. Each `[ VALUE, %PREDECESSOR ]` pairs an incoming value with its source block; it is not an array access. The PHI’s i32 type applies to every incoming value, so a literal inside a bracket does not repeat the type. PHIs go at the start of a block. On a loop’s first entry choose its entry value, and on a back edge choose its carried value. Multiple PHIs select incoming values together, rather than sequentially overwriting each other.

End this function invocation and return the typed operand to its caller. `ret i32 %v` returns the integer value, while `ret ptr ...` returns a pointer. A return does not proceed to the next printed block or automatically go back to dispatch.

Produce a value from `select i1 CONDITION, TYPE TRUE_VALUE, TYPE FALSE_VALUE`. A true condition chooses the first alternative, false the second; alternatives have the same type. This does not branch or conditionally execute the instructions that computed the operands. Here the chosen result is either a destination’s state number or the final return value.

Write memory: in `store i32 VALUE, ptr ADDRESS`, the first operand is the value and the second is the destination address. A store has an effect but no result name. Writing a state slot changes the next routing choice; writing a demotion slot transports an original program value.

Transfer control according to one integer value. The destination immediately after the condition is the default for no matching case. Each line inside `[...]` pairs a typed case constant with `label %DESTINATION`; only one destination is taken. An original switch chooses a program outcome; a dispatcher switch decodes the stored state ID. The brackets are a case list, not a runtime array.

End the block by asserting that execution never reaches this point on a defined run. Actually executing it is undefined behavior; it is not error recovery, a return, or a C++ exception. The state-machine invariant must prevent a bad stored ID from taking this default path.

blocks.text: Keep address, contents, and loaded value separate. For example, an alloca result is the address of a slot; a store writes an integer into that slot; a later load defines a new SSA name for the integer read back. The pointer name does not become the stored number. A value slot preserves program data, whereas ms.state (when present) stores a control-flow destination encoding.
Walk one concrete execution

Call count_to with limit = 2. The initial counter is 0; the signed-less-than test is true for 0 and 1, so the body increments it to 1 and then 2. At 2 the test is false and exit returns 2. A PHI selects initial 0 on entry and the previous body’s next value on a back edge; after demotion the loop-variable slot carries those same values. The complete after listing stores state 0 for header, 1 for body, or 2 for exit. State storage controls where to run; separate value slots carry the counter. The default unreachable path is never an intended outcome.

blocks.title: Read the complete before-and-after LLVM modules

blocks.text: Before — loop original

define i32 @count_to(i32 %limit) {
entry:
  br label %header

header:                                           ; preds = %body, %entry
  %i = phi i32 [ 0, %entry ], [ %next, %body ]
  %continue = icmp slt i32 %i, %limit
  br i1 %continue, label %body, label %exit

body:                                             ; preds = %header
  %next = add i32 %i, 1
  br label %header

exit:                                             ; preds = %header
  ret i32 %i
}
After — loop full

define i32 @count_to(i32 %limit) {
entry:
  %ms.state = alloca i32, align 4
  %i.reload.reg2mem = alloca i32, align 4
  %i.reg2mem = alloca i32, align 4
  store i32 0, ptr %i.reg2mem, align 4
  store i32 0, ptr %ms.state, align 4
  br label %ms.dispatch

header:                                           ; preds = %ms.dispatch
  %i.reload = load i32, ptr %i.reg2mem, align 4
  store i32 %i.reload, ptr %i.reload.reg2mem, align 4
  %i.reload.reload = load i32, ptr %i.reload.reg2mem, align 4
  %continue = icmp slt i32 %i.reload.reload, %limit
  %ms.next = select i1 %continue, i32 1, i32 2
  store i32 %ms.next, ptr %ms.state, align 4
  br label %ms.dispatch

body:                                             ; preds = %ms.dispatch
  %i.reload.reload1 = load i32, ptr %i.reload.reg2mem, align 4
  %next = add i32 %i.reload.reload1, 1
  store i32 %next, ptr %i.reg2mem, align 4
  store i32 0, ptr %ms.state, align 4
  br label %ms.dispatch

exit:                                             ; preds = %ms.dispatch
  %i.reload.reload2 = load i32, ptr %i.reload.reg2mem, align 4
  ret i32 %i.reload.reload2

ms.dispatch:                                      ; preds = %body, %header, %entry
  %ms.current = load i32, ptr %ms.state, align 4
  switch i32 %ms.current, label %ms.invalid [
    i32 0, label %header
    i32 1, label %body
    i32 2, label %exit
  ]

ms.invalid:                                       ; preds = %ms.dispatch
  unreachable
}

Both listings are complete LLVM modules defining the example function, not fragments with omitted blocks. They have no main driver unless one is explicitly included; opt can parse and verify them, while execution requires a caller. Names, alignments, and printer annotations may differ in your own output. These listings were generated and verified with the isolated LLVM 23.1.5 teaching references, not copied from an assumed completed learner implementation.

The integer naming a destination block in our dispatcher; not the same as the block’s optional printed name.

LLVM’s shared context for IR facilities such as uniqued types; obtained here from the function.
